# Great Books and the Future of Humanities Education for Engineers

Great Books are a plausible part of the future of humanities education for engineers, but they are not a sufficient future by themselves. The strongest case is not for a stand-alone canon-based curriculum. It is for using Great Books-style practices—close reading, structured dialogue, moral reflection, and argument across disagreement—inside a broader humanities program tied to engineering practice.

That distinction matters. Engineers need more than cultural literacy. They need to communicate with publics, understand institutions and histories, evaluate ethical risk, and see how technical systems affect communities. A serious curriculum should therefore join seminar-based reading with ethics, public policy, history of technology, communication, and design-based application.

## A Limited but Useful Example: Franciscan Missionaries of Our Lady University

Franciscan Missionaries of Our Lady University’s Bachelor of Arts in Great Books is not an engineering program, so it should not be treated as evidence that Great Books education is spreading through engineering schools. Its relevance is narrower: it shows how a Great Books curriculum can be organized as a coherent undergraduate formation rather than as a loose set of electives.

According to the university catalog and program page, the major is a four-year liberal arts program built around major works from classical antiquity through the contemporary period. The catalog identifies a sequence of Great Books seminars as central to the degree. Program materials also describe seminar-based study, authors from varied traditions, vocational discernment, internships, and a career-oriented minor.

Those claims should be kept modest. The example does not establish a national trend, and it does not supply a ready-made model for engineering. It does, however, identify transferable design principles: sustained reading over time, discussion across disagreement, attention to vocation, and some connection between liberal education and career preparation. Those principles could be adapted within engineering education if they were linked to technical judgment, public responsibility, and sociotechnical case work.

## Why the Humanities Belong in Engineering Formation

The strongest evidence for humanities integration comes from the expectations already placed on engineers. ABET’s Criterion 3 student outcomes include effective communication, teamwork, ethical and professional responsibility, and the ability to consider global, cultural, social, environmental, and economic factors in engineering decisions (ABET, *Criteria for Accrediting Engineering Programs*, Criterion 3). The National Academy of Engineering’s *The Engineer of 2020* similarly argues that engineers will need communication, leadership, ethics, social understanding, and adaptability in addition to technical expertise (NAE, 2004).

ABET and the NAE do not prescribe Great Books education. Their relevance is more general and more important: they show that engineering competence includes judgment about human contexts. The NSPE Code of Ethics points in the same direction by requiring engineers to hold public safety, health, and welfare paramount (NSPE, *Code of Ethics for Engineers*). These are not merely technical obligations. They require interpretation, communication, moral reasoning, and awareness of consequences.

Great Books-style pedagogy can help when it is used for those purposes. Its value is not simply that students encounter famous texts. Its value is that students practice reading carefully, listening charitably, testing claims, and asking what kind of human good a project serves. Literature and philosophy can sharpen attention to responsibility, suffering, ambition, dignity, and moral conflict. History of technology can show how technical systems are shaped by political, economic, and cultural conditions. Rhetoric, writing, ethics, and public policy can help students explain risk, uncertainty, safety, tradeoffs, regulation, justice, and accountability.

A brief hybrid unit illustrates the point. Students might read a text on responsibility, compare it with the NSPE Code of Ethics, analyze an infrastructure failure report or AI design case, and write a public memo explaining the ethical and technical tradeoffs. This would not replace engineering analysis. It would support ABET-aligned capacities: ethical responsibility, public communication, and attention to the social consequences of design.

## Why Great Books Alone Are Not Enough

The question is not whether close-reading seminars are valuable. They are. The question is whether a Great Books-only curriculum can meet the needs of engineers who will work in software, medicine, energy, transportation, water, climate adaptation, infrastructure, and other socially embedded fields.

A narrow or fixed canon would be insufficient for that task. This does not mean every Great Books curriculum is narrow. Some are more plural, historically expansive, and open to revision. For engineering students, that openness is essential. They need older works, but they also need global, contemporary, scientific, and marginalized voices. A stronger model could include classical texts, political theory, religious and philosophical traditions, modern novels, science writing, environmental literature, disability studies, postcolonial writers, and testimony from communities affected by technology. Rigor and plurality can reinforce each other when the curriculum is designed around serious questions rather than inherited prestige alone.

There is also a curricular constraint. Engineering degrees are credit-intensive. A long, separate humanities sequence will not fit every program, and requiring one may crowd out other forms of professional preparation. Many schools will need integrated formats: engineering ethics, technology-and-society courses, design justice, environmental humanities, medical humanities, public policy labs, writing-intensive design studios, and capstone projects with public-facing communication. These formats can preserve the strengths of seminar learning while keeping humanities education close to technical practice.

## Conclusion

Great Books should not be treated as the whole future of humanities education for engineers. They are most valuable as one element in a hybrid model of sociotechnical formation.

The better future combines enduring texts, contemporary voices, historical cases, ethics, policy, communication, and design contexts. Engineers need humanities education that forms ethical imagination and practical judgment where technology actually operates: in institutions, environments, markets, infrastructures, and human communities.

Building a Bridge Between Engineering and the Humanities - Northwestern Now
Building a Bridge Between Engineering and the Humanities
It is in the augmentation of possibilities — the things we never knew existed — where remarkable opportunities exist at the intersection of engineering and humanities.
February 17, 2016
This article originally appeared in The Chronicle of Higher Education on February 14, 2016.
By Julio M. Ottino and Gary Saul Morson
The engineering field is booming these days. Society regards it as an essential part of innovation, and colleges promote a degree in it as an entry into a fruitful, sustaining career. The humanities, by contrast, are in peril, with fewer students each year.
We want to bridge this divide and help create a system where the two areas are not separate but are essential to each other. One of us began his studies in art and is now dean of an engineering school, and the other is an expert in Russian literature who originally planned to study physics.
We know that engineering and the humanities differ not just in subject matter but in the very kinds of thinking they encourage. So the question is not just what information from each domain might be useful to the other, but also what each could learn by imagining the world in a whole new way.
In the United States, we are uniquely positioned to bring these two cultures together because, unlike in Europe and South America, students here are expected to learn much more than their specialty. This makes interdisciplinary interactions involving the left brain — analytical, convergent, and quantitative skills associated with science and engineering — and right brain — artistic and humanistic abilities — easier to achieve. Doing so will result in much more talented and versatile engineers and humanists, but it will require vast changes at every level.
By its very nature, engineering is creative and directed to human uses. All too often, however, engineering education postpones or overlooks both. Instead, it is presented as a process of absorption, followed only much later by the production of something new.
Students master routine solving of well-understood problems. Textbooks present current knowledge as timeless truths, as if they had been handed down by divine revelation. Students are told to be creative only at the very end of their studies, in a senior thesis or a design project. Imagine if poets were trained to identify meters but to suspend actually using them to create a poem for several years.
Fortunately, teaching in engineering has evolved significantly over the past decade or so, though not in all places and not all at the same rate. Instead of simply passing on knowledge, the best programs now try to foster experiential learning. Teams rule, and in place of homogenous courses with all engineers in the same discipline, new courses pull together teams from multiple disciplines, including many outside of engineering.
In the arts and humanities, creative and metaphorical thinking come into play early on. Basic literature courses do not teach mastery of a body of material — not just because there is no such body but because it isn’t clear what "mastery of material" would mean. Literature does not aspire to transfer information per se; one must get personally involved.
From the first day of class, the good literature professor does not try to transfer knowledge about poems but models the process of imaginative interpretation of a poem. Good literature lectures are a form of improvisational performance exhibiting what it is like to experience a story, a novel, or a great painting, and arrive at an interpretation. That is the real lesson, not the interpretation itself.
What if more engineers contemplated their work similarly? By the same token, if humanists understood how scientists and engineers think, and if they were not mystified by mathematics, experimentation, and the testing characteristic of those disciplines, they would appreciate their own distinctive ways of thinking and grasp opportunities to contribute something distinctive.
The Russian Formalist critic Victor ­Shklovsky argued that art demands we reverse the usual process of learning. When we acquire a skill, we normally practice it until it is automatic. Learning is, in this sense, a process of familiarization. But sometimes it is important to experience something that has long grown familiar as if for the first time.
Or, as Shklovsky explains, we need to defamiliarize the familiar: "The purpose of art is to impart the sensation of things as they are perceived and not as they are already known. The technique of art is to make objects ‘unfamiliar.’"
Acquiring the habit of overcoming habitual perception is one process that brings engineering and the arts together. It is how great writers impart human experience in new ways, and it is how engineers innovate. Technology does not proceed along a preordained single path, as one might suppose from a textbook or problem-solving approach. Like literature, engineering sometimes works not by satisfying recognized needs but by creating the needs it satisfies. And that is also like literature: Tolstoy did not satisfy someone’s need for a novel called Anna Karenina.
But Tolstoy did provide his readers with a glimpse into Anna’s inner life. Similarly, engineering thrives by going beyond the technical into the realm of its human users. More and more, engineering education is recognizing the importance of understanding devices, systems, and processes in terms of the people who use them.
At the heart of human-centered design is empathy, and empathy is what literature, above all, is good at teaching. When you read a great novel, you identify with a character, experience what she is experiencing, follow her thoughts and feelings moment by moment from within. You do this with people of a different culture, age, gender, social class, nationality, profession, and religion. You do it with several characters in the course of one long novel, and not just once, but countless times, until it becomes a habit. Empathy creates better people and better technical innovations for people to use.
So how do we ensure that more skillful innovators emerge from academe?
Boosting enrollments in STEM is not enough. An educational system that merges humanities and sciences, creating whole-brain engineers and scientifically inspired humanists, fosters more than just innovation. It yields more-flexible individuals who adapt to unanticipated changes as the world evolves unpredictably.
But it is easy to see why existing systems encourage the opposite. One reason is funding. Most doctoral students in engineering are paid to go to school, with funding provided by government grants. The demand for results, the expanding list of compliance mechanisms, and the gravitational pull toward meeting narrow program goals create a closed system that allows little time or attention for ancillary pursuits. This process discourages whole-brainers from even applying.
Alternative graduate programs should cultivate the whole-brain experience that is more often seen at the undergraduate level. One avenue is to provide courses that bring different modes of thinking, rather than moving students in parallel, noninteractive tracks. At our institution we have encouraged that kind of thinking in courses that link engineers with artists, both within our university and with the School of the Art Institute of Chicago.
It should not be rare to have graduate students in science and engineering in literature, philosophy, and history of science courses. It should be the norm. It is in the augmentation of possibilities — the things we never knew existed — where remarkable opportunities exist at the intersection of engineering and humanities. The possibilities are vast.
Julio M. Ottino is dean of the Robert R. McCormick School of Engineering and Applied Science, and Gary Saul Morson is a professor of Slavic languages and literature,

I assume you're asking how a black hole can evaporate due to Hawking radiation. The answer is that the Hawking radiation does not come from the event horizon, but instead comes from a region just outside the event horizon so time has not stopped at its position.

Say you're a distant observer having your own clock and you're observing a clock falling into the black hole. As the clock approaches the black hole, the time measured by you is much slower than your own clock. As it nears the event-horizon, it gets red-shifted so much and at its closest distance to the horizon (somehow you managed to see the red-shifted clock), you'll see the clock freeze and stands still there. This results in a scene that you'll see the clock stay there forever, never reaching the event-horizon. (The same thing happens during the formation of a blackhole)
But if you are an "in-falling observer" along with the clock, you'll see that your clock is normal. Even after you've fallen into the blackhole, you can see your own clock tick. But, you can't quite determine whether you've crossed the horizon or not..! So, this kinda (local) observation does not account for the blackhole's age anyway.

The short answer is: time does not stop for something falling into a black hole. It only appears to slow down from the viewpoint of someone far away.

There are two different clocks being compared:

1. The clock far away

An outside observer watching a clock fall toward the black hole sees the falling clock run slower and slower. The light from that clock also becomes more and more redshifted. Near the event horizon, the signal becomes extremely delayed and faint, so the clock appears to freeze there.

This is an appearance caused by gravitational time dilation and by how light escapes from near the horizon. It does not mean the falling clock itself has stopped.

2. The clock falling in

For the person or clock falling into the black hole, time continues normally. Their own wristwatch ticks as usual. In general relativity this is called their proper time. They can cross the event horizon in a finite amount of proper time.

For a very large black hole, crossing the horizon may not feel locally special at that exact moment. The dangerous part is not that time stops, but that tidal forces and the path toward the singularity become unavoidable once inside.

Now for the lifetime of the black hole:

The quoted lifetime of a black hole, such as an evaporation time due to Hawking radiation, is normally measured using the time of distant observers. Hawking radiation is not best thought of as a normal process happening “inside the black hole” that requires an internal clock at the singularity. It is a quantum effect of fields in curved spacetime, associated with the region outside or near the horizon.

So there is no contradiction:

- To a distant observer, infalling matter appears to slow, redshift, and fade.
- To the falling matter, its own time keeps passing.
- The black hole’s evaporation time is an outside-observer description.
- The event horizon is a global feature of spacetime, not simply a visible surface that must be seen forming in finite telescope time.

A careful wording is therefore: “A distant observer never receives a clear signal of the object crossing the horizon,” not “time literally stops everywhere at the horizon.”

For more background, see standard general relativity treatments such as Sean Carroll’s Spacetime and Geometry or Misner, Thorne, and Wheeler’s Gravitation. For accessible summaries, NASA and ESA black-hole resources describe event horizons and gravitational redshift. Hawking radiation was introduced in S. W. Hawking, “Particle Creation by Black Holes,” Communications in Mathematical Physics 43, 199–220, 1975.

Kuch Rang Pyar Ke Aise Bhi (English Title: Shades Of Love) is an Indian Hindi -language romantic drama television series which aired on 29 February 2016 to 12 November 2021 on Sony Entertainment Television. It stars Erica Fernandes, Shaheer Sheikh and Supriya Pilgaonkar.[1] [2]
The second season of the show aired from 25 September 2017 to 2 November 2017 lasting for 26 episodes. A third season Kuch Rang Pyar Ke Aise Bhi: Nayi Kahaani started airing on SET India on 12 July 2021. Post leap, the show was about the journey of the characters to their maturation. Some of the highlights are understanding, realizations, character developments, and a matured edition of reunion of separated lovers. [3]

Plot[edit]
Season 1[edit]
The show explores work in progress relationship of Sonakshi "Sona" Bose and Devrath "Dev" Dixit. Dev lost his father at a young age and hence his mother brought up him and his three sisters singlehandedly. Seeing his mother struggle so much despite of all the hardships made him deeply venerate her. But due to unfavourable financial circumstances she could only educate Dev and his younger sister Neha was left at home to take care of his two younger sisters. Now Dev is a successful business tycoon who lives with his mother Ishwari and three sisters, Neha, Riya and Nikki. Dev owes everything to his mother and has a feeling of indebtedness and complete devotion for her. But Neha, though loves her family, still has resentment in her heart and feels that her mother has done partiality among her children, only educating Dev and depriving her of any opportunities. Neha confronts her mother and accused her of ruining her happiness, saying "You may have beget four children but without feigning you are mother of only one". Hearing her harsh words, Ishwari faints and Dev calls a doctor. Dr. Sinha tells him that his mother has history of such fatigue due to improper nutrition and recommends him a nutritional consultant, Dr. Sonakshi Bose. Dr. Sonakshi is a quick-witted, lively young doctor who is from a Kolkata-based, Bengali family of five living in Delhi.
Sona is a young and vibrant nutritionist who is hired by Dev to take care of Ishwari's health. Dev and Sonakshi get off on the wrong foot. She thinks of him as rude and he thinks of her as stubborn. Due to an accident, Dev cares for Sona and she falls for him. Sparks fly between Sona and Dev and they fall in love. When Ishwari learns of their relationship she is heartbroken as she fears that she will be replaced by Sona in Dev's life. When Dev realizes that his mother does not approve of this relationship, he takes a practical decision and decides to part ways. Ishwari realizes that Dev cannot be happy without Sona, and agrees to their marriage. Sona and Dev reconcile and get married. Neha also marries her former English teacher, Ranveer. After heated arguments between Sona and Dev due to Ishwari's continuous interference in their married life and misunderstandings created by Dev's cousin, Vicky, Sonakshi and Dev part ways.
7 Years Later[edit]
Sona is now a successful businesswoman living in Kolkata with her family and six-year-old daughter Suhana, while Dev becomes a Casanova, not knowing that he and Sona have a daughter. She shifts to Delhi for business purposes and buys a portion of Dev's office. Sona keeps hiding Suhana from Dev as she feels that he might snatch Suhana away from her. Eventually, while befriending Suhana as she and his nephew Golu study in the same school, Dev sees her with Sona and finds the truth about her. They both decide to be with each other for Suhana's sake. Sonakshi's brother Saurav marries Ronita. Meanwhile, Ishwari starts liking Sona after saving her from a mysterious person named Khatri. During all this, Dev and Sona realize that they still love each other, and reunite. Sonakshi helps Dev correcting his mistakes he had done in those seven years and hence brings all the members of the Dixit family back together. Sonakshi also lands up in a trouble and Dev saves her just in time, making Dev overprotective of her. She and Dev then find out that Vicky was the main cause for all their misunderstandings, and he later apologizes. Sonakshi gets pregnant again.
Season 1 ends on a happy note with Sona giving birth to their second child Shubh, with the entire family united.
Season 2[edit]
This season explores the life of Sona and Dev after the birth of their second child, Shubh. Dev quits his business temporarily to let Sona pursue her dream, much to Ishwari's dismay. It shows Sona a working woman and Dev as a househusband.
The season also focuses on how Dev changes the education pattern of their children's school and how Suhana and Golu fall victim to a dangerous game. It also focuses on Saurabh and Ronita's experience as first-time parents.
Dev then becomes an RJ and the family celebrates his success. Season 2 ends as Shubh says Maa and Papa for the first time.
